title: Promise and Pitfalls of Practitioner Action Research, Part 2
author: Jonathan Firth
summary: In this second installment on practitioner action research, Jonathan Firth revisits the promise and risks of teachers studying their own classroom practice. He argues that while grounded, context-specific research feels more relevant than the broader literature, it is prone to confirmation bias because practitioners typically study interventions they already believe in, using small samples and weak methodology. Using a hypothetical teacher named Bob who tests the spacing effect and finds no benefit, Firth demonstrates how a null result from an underpowered classroom study is far more likely to be a false negative than genuine evidence overturning decades of memory research. He clarifies that this skepticism does not contradict his own 2019 book on teacher research, which emphasizes engaging with existing evidence over generating new studies, and closes by weighing action research against other uses of a teacher's limited time, such as building explanation and questioning skills. Firth ultimately endorses action research as valuable for building methodological literacy, provided its findings are held loosely.
points: Action research's central risk is confirmation bias: interventions tend to be studied by practitioners who already believe in them, compounding with weak classroom-level methodology.

The Bob/spacing-effect scenario illustrates how a null result from a small, uncontrolled classroom study is far more likely a false negative than evidence overturning established research on learning and memory.
Firth argues teachers often gain more from engaging with existing systematic reviews of research than from running their own underpowered studies on the same question.
Time spent on action research competes directly with other high-value uses of teacher time -- reading research, refining classroom management, and improving explanations and questioning.
Despite the risks, Firth still endorses action research as valuable for building research literacy and motivation, as long as teachers avoid over-interpreting their own findings.
quotes: However, as I raised in my earlier post, there are real risks of bias. Many interventions are studied by practitioners that already think that they are a good idea.

Consider, for example, the idea of flipped classrooms or technology use - they tend to be researched by enthusiasts rather than sceptics. Coupled with rather wobbly research methodology, and there is a lot of potential for educators to see what they want to see.

That would actually be a major mistake. We know from the broader research literature that the spacing effect does work. This leads two possibilities: there is something about Bob's context that is so unique that it overturns decades of research on learning and memory; or the experiment was flawed, leading to a false negative.

The problems are exacerbated by the fact that most teachers are not experts in research methodology and statistics, and may lack experience, too. That is before we consider issues about research ethics, which are also riskier with inexperienced researchers.

Take reading, for example. I think that a primary school teacher would be much better off reading reputable systematic reviews of research into reading than trying to figure out how reading develops via action research with their own class.
So, I'm perfectly happy for all educators to engage in action research. I'd just warn against reading too much into findings - at least while one's understanding of methodology is still developing.
